A thermometer that goes below

Argo floats change their buoyancy to sink and rise. In a typical cycle, they drift at depth, dive, then take a vertical series of measurements as they ascend. Each ascent makes a profile—a thin glimpse of a very large ocean.

03 / What the surface leaves out

Warmth has
a vertical shape.

Surface heating can build a warm upper layer. Cooling and mixing can alter how far that layer reaches. The zone where temperature changes quickly with depth is a thermocline.

The ocean’s “memory” lives in this structure: a surface reading cannot describe what lies below, or how that water may interact with the surface later.

These profiles show changing structure, not its single cause. The floats also move through currents and different water masses. Temperature alone does not determine density; salinity matters too. This is not a measurement of global warming, net heat uptake, or a formal mixed-layer depth.

Open the data, methods & limits — 495 profiles, 53,454 measurements

What is actually here

Three editorially selected floats, chosen for contrasting Atlantic histories and accessible delayed-mode records: 6902755 and 6902756 (ASFAR), and 6902746 (CORIOLIS). All ascending profile records in their retrieved multi-profile files are available here, including the empty record. This is a case-study collection, not a representative ocean sample.

496 input profiles → 1 descending profile omitted → 495 ascents. Of 53,802 levels with a reported raw or adjusted pressure in those ascents, 53,454 meet the display policy. 347 levels fall outside 0–2,000 dbar and 1 has missing or rejected data. One ascent has no accepted samples.

Quality and units

Use DATA_MODE=D, JULD_QC=1 and POSITION_QC=1. At each level, adjusted pressure and adjusted in-situ temperature must both have QC=1, finite error estimates, pressure error <20 dbar and temperature error ≤0.01°C. Salinity is shown separately only with adjusted QC=1 and error ≤0.05. No under-ice estimated positions are used. The exact errors remain inspectable.

Pressure is in dbar; it has not been converted to metres. Temperature is adjusted in-situ temperature on ITS-90, not potential or Conservative Temperature. Practical salinity is not Absolute Salinity. No heat content, density or mixed-layer calculation is made.

Argo file and QC guide ↗ · Argo accuracy guidance ↗

How the pictures are made

The profile lines connect adjacent accepted samples as a visual guide; they do not imply continuous measurement. They break across rejected samples and gaps wider than 100 dbar. The archive draws separate marks at actual sample pressures and actual profile times. It never fills between profiles or extrapolates below a cast.

Probe readouts always snap to the nearest accepted measurement within 15 dbar in the upper-ocean views, or 60 dbar in the 2,000-dbar view. Each readout labels the actual sampled pressure. No interpolation is used. Time is UTC. Map links connect reported locations, not tracked underwater paths. Endpoint distance is a spherical great-circle estimate using radius 6,371.0088 km, not distance traveled.

The opening pair was selected for nearly matching near-surface temperatures and close reported positions. It is not the largest contrast in the archive. Its 5-dbar difference is 0.066°C; at 95 dbar, 1.446°C; at 195 dbar, November is 0.466°C colder.
